lines.text: Thieves used to copy your bank card in seconds. Then a tiny gold chip showed up, and copying almost stopped. Why?
The old magnetic stripe is like a sticker with your details written on it. Same data, every single time. Swipe it once, and anyone can copy it.
The chip is different. It's a tiny computer, with a secret key locked inside that never comes out.
When you pay, the terminal sends the chip a fresh random number, plus the amount and the time.
The chip mixes them with its secret key, and answers with a one-time code. A cryptogram.
Your bank has a copy of the key, so it checks the code. Match? Approved.
Next time, the number is different, so the code is different. Copy one, and it's useless the next second.
And the chip is built to destroy its secrets if someone tries to cut it open.
Orbi Transfer works the same way: every file gets its own QR code and its own passcode. Scan it, type the passcode, and only then does it unlock.
